text:
## Observations

1. The minimum number of erasures equals the number of maximal runs of consecutive values among the distinct values in the subarray.
2. A present value \(x\) starts a run exactly when \(x-1\) is absent.
3. At a fixed right endpoint \(R\), a value \(x\) appears in \([L,R]\) exactly when \(L\le \operatorname{last}[x]\), where \(\operatorname{last}[x]\) is its latest position at or before \(R\), or zero if it has yet to appear.
4. Extending the right endpoint by a value \(v\) changes only \(\operatorname{last}[v]\), so only the run-start contributions for \(v\) and \(v+1\) can change.

## Solution sketch

> The minimum number of erasures equals the number of maximal runs of consecutive values among the distinct values in the subarray.

1. Reduce the problem to counting runs. A missing value between two runs stays missing throughout the erasures, so a single operation can cover values from only one original run. Erasing each full run in one operation attains this lower bound. Every occurrence of a value is erased together, so duplicates need no separate handling.

> A present value \(x\) starts a run exactly when \(x-1\) is absent.

2. Count each run once, through its smallest value. For each right endpoint \(R\), let \(S\) be the total number of run starts across all subarrays ending at \(R\). Summing \(S\) over the scan gives the answer.

> At a fixed right endpoint \(R\), a value \(x\) appears in \([L,R]\) exactly when \(L\le \operatorname{last}[x]\), where \(\operatorname{last}[x]\) is its latest position at or before \(R\), or zero if it has yet to appear.

3. For each \(x\) from \(1\) through \(N\), its contribution to \(S\) is the number of left endpoints satisfying \(\operatorname{last}[x-1]<L\le \operatorname{last}[x]\). This count is \(\max(0,\operatorname{last}[x]-\operatorname{last}[x-1])\). Initialize the last-position array to zero, keep \(\operatorname{last}[0]=0\) because value \(0\) is absent, and initialize \(S\) and the answer to zero.

> Extending the right endpoint by a value \(v\) changes only \(\operatorname{last}[v]\), so only the run-start contributions for \(v\) and \(v+1\) can change.

4. Scan the sequence using 1-based positions. At position \(R\) with value \(v\), subtract the old contributions for \(v\) and, if \(v<N\), \(v+1\). Set \(\operatorname{last}[v]=R\), add the updated contributions for those same values, and add \(S\) to the answer. After the scan, print the answer. This also handles repeated values and \(N=1\) through the same update. Each position takes constant time, so the algorithm uses \(O(N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space.

generation.note: Harness wall time includes Codex startup; not API latency.

usage.note: Codex token counts include its harness context; not comparable to API usage.

isolation.mechanism: codex exec, fresh ephemeral session, empty temporary working directory, user config and exec rules ignored, read-only sandbox, web search and listed features disabled, credential-like variables removed from the environment
isolation.limits: Codex harness instructions and its own tool descriptions remain in the model context; they cannot be removed. Tool isolation is verified post hoc from the event stream, which contained no tool, command, file or search events.
